Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

npmatch (development version)

The normalizer now comes from npnormalize. The next release is 0.2.0.

  • What moved. npmatch’s normalizer moved, unchanged, into the new npnormalize package, which npmatch now imports. That covers:
    • the rule tables;
    • np_normalize(), np_name_core() and np_name_placeholder();
    • the corpus statistics (np_name_freq(), np_token_idf(), np_addr_freq(), np_stopwords());
    • the blocking tokenizer;
    • np_normalize_signature().
  • Nothing changes for callers. npmatch re-exports those nine functions, so npmatch::np_normalize(), scripts, pfmatch and networked990 work as before.
  • The move itself kept every stored artifact valid, because np_normalize_signature() still reported v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e on both sides of it — npmatch 0.1.1 and npnormalize 0.1.0 and 0.1.1.
  • npnormalize has since moved the signature on purpose, more than once. 0.1.2 made BUILDING a unit designator (npnormalize#7), and 0.1.3 made a line naming several units keep the most specific one and the house number a whole token — v1-592912060053c4c3 at that point. Stored street_unit, street_unit_id, street_num and street_name values from before that must be rebuilt — matchdb’s database, bundles and tranches included (matchdb#29). npmatch carries a version floor on npnormalize, so an install cannot quietly compute keys with an older normalizer than the one it is pinned to.
  • The floor is npnormalize (>= 0.1.7), and the four releases it reaches for have all landed on npnormalize’s main. 0.1.4 added street_has_box — whether a street carries a box component, which is_po_box cannot answer because it is the gate that blanks the address key (npnormalize#9); 0.1.5 published one box vocabulary for the four packages that had each kept their own, which also made a lettered box (PO BOX A) a box (npnormalize#12); and 0.1.6 widened that vocabulary to the long-tail spellings (PO BX, PB, P BOX, POSTAL DRAWER, POSTAL OFC BOX, APDO), made a mail-only line blank the address key rather than key it — general delivery, military mail, a bare drawer, none of which is a building two organizations share — and added mail_key, the box plus its ZIP, which is the one co-location signal a blanked box still carries (npnormalize#13); and 0.1.7 made a hyphen inside a leading house number close up rather than become a space, so the two filed spellings of one Queens or Hawaii address reach one street_key and street_num stops truncating at the hyphen, and folded eleven further spellings of FOUNDATION — three of them the word broken across two tokens by a line break, which is why np_name_rules() now returns a split_words table that a port must apply before abbrev (npnormalize#16, npnormalize#17). Each move changed the signature, so tests/testthat/test-signature.R now pins v1-59c6e84c5f38e9f5, read off npnormalize’s merged main rather than off a value copied out of a branch; the registry comment beside it keeps every earlier value as part of the record. Stored keys and the statistics built on them need rebuilding once more, matchdb’s published data included.
  • Why. Both sides of a match depend on the normalizer: matchdb stores its keys, and npmatch computes them for each query. With the normalizer in its own package, matchdb no longer needs npmatch, and npmatch can depend on matchdb in turn.
  • Where things are now:
    • The normalizer’s tests live in npnormalize. npmatch keeps the tests that block, compare or score on top of it, and adds one checking that its signature and re-exported functions are npnormalize’s own.
    • The five name comparators that sat beside the normalizer moved to R/compare.R, since they feed np_compare() and precompute nothing.
    • npmatch’s blocking and comparison call npnormalize’s exported np_tokenize(), np_doc_freq(), np_addr_key() and np_state_abb().
  • Dependencies: stringi is no longer imported (only the normalizer used it); npnormalize is, from GitHub (Remotes:).
  • street_has_box is read by nothing, on purpose. npnormalize 0.1.4 names npmatch as the column’s intended consumer, and the measurement says npmatch has no use for it: on the 304,274-pair labeled benchmark, street_has_box disagreeing across a pair while geo_stnum == 1 selects 29 pairs, and they are exactly the 29 that is_po_box — which npmatch already reads, as geo_pobox — already selects. All 29 fail .np_hier_score()’s street_sim >= 0.9 floor, so street_hit cannot fire on one. The reason is that the same release anchored .np_parse_street()’s gate, so a street that merely carries a box keeps its house number: across the 3,687,435-row unified BMF, street_num holds a box number on 0 rows where is_po_box is FALSE. (Measured under both 0.1.4 and the 0.1.5 that landed during the work, which only narrows the slice where the two columns differ, from 11,982 rows to 10,984.) A veto on a disagreeing flag would also be wrong, not idle — it refuses 211 EMMET ST S PO BOX against 211 EMMET ST S, one building whose house number is genuinely 211 on both sides. tests/testthat/test-box-component.R pins all of that, including the must-still-match pair, so a regression in npnormalize’s parse fails npmatch’s suite instead of passing quietly; dev/STREET-HAS-BOX.md carries the full measurement and the two conditions that would reopen it. Nothing in the compared field set, the scorer or the veto rules changed, so attr(pairs, "cmp_cols") and stored models are untouched.

matchdb references and precomputed address counts

  • np_cascade() and np_run_batches() take a matchdb reference directly. Pass the object matchdb::md_compile() or matchdb::md_reference() returns as reference, and npmatch uses its frame plus whichever of name_freq, token_idf, ref_index and addr_freq it carries, instead of recomputing them. Explicit arguments still take precedence. A reference whose normalizer signature differs from the installed one is refused. npmatch recognises the object by its shape, so matchdb is not a dependency, not even a suggested one.
  • Both take an addr_freq argument, a precomputed np_addr_freq() table. np_cascade() used to recount it on every call, over whatever reference it was given. Pass one counted over the full reference when matching against part of it, so crowded addresses are not under-counted. matchdb’s bundles ship one counted over exactly the bundle’s rows.
  • np_run_batches() counts addresses once for the whole run and keeps the table in its cache = file. A cache written before this version gains it on first use, as an older cache already gained ref_index.

The suite a reviewer is shown

  • A bare # now agrees with PMB in geo_unit_same_kind, as well as with the room-level designators. Since npnormalize 0.1.3 a line naming several units keeps the most specific, so a mail store’s STE 204 # 22915 keeps the customer’s box as # 22915; against a record written PMB 22915, the reviewer was told “not the same kind of unit” about one mailbox. # is either a door or a box, so it agrees with both, while PMB 136 against STE 136 and FL 2 against STE 2 still do not. No score moves.

  • A reviewer is no longer told that a floor is the same suite as a suite (#23, reported from pfmatch via npnormalize#7). geo_unit compares npnormalize’s street_unit_id, which drops the designator — that is what makes STE 320 and # 320 agree, one office written two ways, and it is right. The same drop made FL 2 agree with STE 2, and PMB 136 with STE 136:

    query reference geo_unit prompt, before prompt, now
    FL 2 STE 2 1 same suite not the same kind of unit
    PMB 136 STE 136 1 same suite not the same kind of unit
    STE 320 # 320 1 same suite same suite

    np_compare() now also returns geo_unit_same_kind — 1 both sides name the same kind of place, 0 they do not, NA either side names no unit — and np_as_prompt() requires it before it says the suites are the same. The room-level designators (STE APT UNIT RM SPC TRLR LOT #) are one kind; a floor, a mailbox, a department, a building and a basement are each their own. A review frame saved before the column existed reads correctly too, because the canonical values are in the frame.

  • No score moves. np_score() reads geo_unit and nothing else, so the 0.97 suite credit and its multi-tenant gate are exactly as they were; a test asserts the scores are identical with the new column dropped. The grouping deliberately stays in npmatch: which designators count as the same door is a matching policy, while npnormalize’s tables feed the normalizer signature that stamps every published artifact. ## Documentation reframed around the six tiers

  • npmatch is documented as a tiered workflow, not as a SAM-to-BMF matcher. The README, the landing page, the package help and the articles now name the six steps the package manages — alias enumeration (matchdb), input standardization (npnormalize), data pre-prep (tokenization, inverse document frequency, name and address frequency), candidate generation by blocking and fuzzy comparison (reclin2), tiered adjudication, and packaging for human or LLM review — and present federal registrants against the IRS Business Master File as the deployment npmatch ships wired for rather than as what it is for. np_map_sam() / np_map_bmf() and the SAM helpers are described as that deployment’s conveniences; pfmatch is named as another deployment.

  • The README and landing page carry a dependency diagram of npmatch, npnormalize, matchdb and reclin2, with a table saying what each owns and why it is separate. pkgdown now renders mermaid blocks on the home page.

  • matchdb is documented as the default reference path. The quick start downloads a published bundle and passes it straight to the cascade; building a reference from raw NCCS files is kept as the path for a vintage, slice or schema matchdb does not publish. The Workflow article leads with it.

  • The README no longer restates npnormalize’s rules. The subroutine-level walkthrough of the normalizer is replaced by the columns it produces and a pointer to npnormalize’s own reference, which is authoritative. The tier-3 corpus statistics get a section of their own, including the warning against counting them over a slice.

  • The prose quotes no normalizer signature. The entry above names the values deliberately, as the record of what moved, and tests/testthat/test-signature.R pins the current one so an unintended move cannot pass unnoticed. Prose that merely asserts a signature is unchanged goes stale instead, which is what had happened here: the README and the Workflow article now say to read the value from np_normalize_signature() and to record what a run reported.

  • The nine normalizer topics collapsed into one reexports page when the normalizer moved, so _pkgdown.yml redirects their old URLs to it, and np_cluster_rollup() / np_pair_links() are in the reference index for the first time.

  • dev/BENCHMARK-RANK-DEFICIENCY.md records the long-standing rank-deficient-fit warning in the np_benchmark() test — which fold degenerates and why, that np_train()’s blanket suppressWarnings() is the part worth fixing, and a plan. dev/probe-rank-deficiency.R reproduces it.

npmatch 0.1.1

Tagged v0.1.1. This is the last npmatch that carries its own normalizer. In the next version the normalizer moves, unchanged, into the npnormalize package, which npmatch then imports and re-exports. Pin this release (in renv, or with @v0.1.1) for anything that should reproduce results from before that move.

  • The normalizer signature at this release is v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e. It is the signature matchdb’s 2026-10-26 release was built with, and the one npnormalize 0.1.0 reproduces.
  • Everything since 0.1.0 is listed below: address and suite classification, the suite identifier, and the name-normalization fixes.

Address and suite normalization

  • np_addr_freq() classifies each shared address, because what a shared address is decides what its evidence is worth, and counts alone cannot tell the kinds apart. It now takes name_keys and adds n_names, top_name_share, unit_coverage and class: federated (many records, one name dominating — a national office its chapters file from, where the address matches every chapter equally and the chapter number is the only discriminator), shared (many records, many names — a fiscal sponsor or registered agent), building (many records across several recorded suites — the suite discriminates) or cluster (a handful, usually an org with its foundation). Over the unified BMF: 1,188 federated addresses holding 60,064 records, 1,319 shared holding 29,910, 1,910 buildings holding 36,327, and 134,212 clusters. np_compare() carries addr_class, addr_top_name_share and addr_unit_coverage per pair and states the class in addr_note, which reaches the review frame, the stage 2 packet and np_as_prompt().

  • The suite credit is additionally gated on unit_coverage (default 0.5): at the BMF addresses holding 10 or more records the share of records naming a suite averages 0.52 and 1,601 of them name none, so “two or more distinct suites here” can describe the data rather than the building. This withholds the credit at 445 of the 23,310 addresses listing two or more suites (1.9%).

  • Damping the street credit at low-discrimination addresses was measured and rejected, against an earlier recommendation of our own. With the street evidence zeroed at crowded addresses, the 304,274 labeled pairs give AUC 0.9981 to 0.9981, precision 0.5669 to 0.5669, recall 0.9212 to 0.9212 and 1,898 YES-band pairs either way — not one decision changes. The geo terms combine with max() and the top rungs sit 0.05 apart, so removing one moves a total score by 0.02; and the two crowded archetypes want opposite treatment, since at a sponsor address the name separates cleanly and damping would only pull the true match down. See dev/MATCHDB-ADDRESS-UNIQUENESS.md section 9.

  • np_addr_freq() is covered by the normalizer signature, so these changes move it again. Read the value with np_normalize_signature() on the commit you are building from, rather than from any value quoted here. The signature is computed over the whole registered normalize path, so a change merging alongside this one moves it too: this entry previously named a value measured on the feature branch, and a one-line .np_replace_tokens() fix that landed in between made it wrong before the merge was a day old. A literal is only safe in a tagged release note, where the commit is pinned.

  • The suite number is parsed properly, carried through to review, and used as evidence where it means something. Previously it was extracted, stripped from street_key, and then dropped: nothing downstream saw it, so neither a human reviewer nor the stage 2 adjudicator could tell two tenants of one building apart.

  • np_normalize() adds street_unit_id, the identifier alone with separators dropped (STE D-2 -> D2). Records are compared on it, so a BMF STE 300 and a source # 300 are recognised as one office, while 320 and 380 are simply different — a suite is an identifier, and a fuzzy score between two of them means nothing.

  • street_unit is now read from the unit column (a second address line) when the street line names no suite. Ignoring it was a penalty rather than a gap: SAM keeps the suite in physical_address_line_2, np_detect_geo() selected the street_unit_full profile on that column’s coverage, and the compared column was then NA on every row — a unit similarity of 0 on every pair, fired precisely because the data was present.

  • A profile requiring unit is no longer auto-selected, because the per-profile weights are a weighted sum, where a field earns its weight only by matching and an unrecorded suite is therefore a silent penalty. Suite evidence now enters np_score(method = "hier"), where the geo terms combine with max() so an absent, differing or crowded suite costs a pair nothing. street_unit_full remains available via an explicit profile =.

  • New np_addr_freq() counts, over the reference, the records at each address, at each address + suite, and the distinct suites per address. np_compare() annotates every pair with geo_unit (1 same suite / 0 different / NA unknown), addr_shared, addr_units, addr_unit_shared and a reviewer-facing addr_note, and np_default_geo_weights() gains unit = 0.97. A matching suite is credited only where it discriminates: several distinct suites on record at that address (a multi-tenant building, where an exact-address match surfaces every tenant) and that suite not itself shared by more than share_min records (a fiscal sponsor or registered agent, where a shared suite says nothing). The crowded cases are reported to the reviewer instead — “12 records share this address and suite” — in the review frame, the stage 2 packet and np_as_prompt().

  • The unit pattern is rebuilt from a .np_unit_designators table and now requires a word boundary and, before an alphabetic id, a separator. Measured on the 1.92M-row unified BMF (dev/scan-unit-designators.R), the old pattern produced a false unit on 27,954 rows (11.3% of all extractions) by matching inside ordinary words — SHERMAN WAY gave room “AN WAY” and INDIGO BROOM LOOP keyed as 10317 INDIGO B — and in 3,636 of them the false match also masked the real unit: 259 N RADNOR CHESTER RD STE 150 extracted STER, from inside CHESTER.

  • Designators added, by volume in the BMF: PMB, FL / FLOOR (including the postfix form, 2ND FLOOR -> FL 2), SPC / SPACE, LOT, TRLR, DEPT, STOP, LBBY, HNGR, BSMT, NUM / NUMBER. USPS C2’s FRNT, REAR, LOWR, UPPR, OFC, PH, PIER, KEY, SIDE and SLIP are left out because in this corpus they match street names, and NO because it is North far more often than Number.

  • The # form is stripped from street_key at last: extraction allowed # and the key strip did not, so 123 MAIN ST # 300 recorded unit # 300 and keyed as 123 MAIN ST 300. Both now run off one pattern, before cleaning, which is the only point at which the # still exists.

  • np_as_prompt() could not run at all: it addressed the pipeline column names (score, name_sim) on a review frame that renames them (total_score, name_similarity), so order(-NULL) errored. Its test had been skipping past the call for the same reason — the id column is renamed too — and now runs.

Name normalization

  • Letters that are not an accented form of another letter now fold to their ASCII spelling: ß → SS, Ø → O, Ł → L, Đ → D, Æ → AE, Œ → OE, Þ → TH. De-accenting cannot reach them, and an unmapped letter was replaced by a space, which split the word it sat in: Straße Fund normalized to STRA E FUND. Folding now runs before the upper-casing, which is what let the eszett through — R’s toupper() is per-character, so it left a letter whose upper case is two letters alone. This is the list matchdb’s md_light_key() folds, so a cached reference key and a run-time query key agree character for character; np_name_rules() returns it as special_letters. np_normalize_signature() changes with it, so any cached name_key / street_key artifact must be rebuilt.
  • 16 more abbreviations expand, taken from networked990’s 990 name resolver and checked against the BMF: FDN / FND / FNDTN / FDTN (FOUNDATION), HOSP, MED, HLTH, HLTHCARE, MGMT, REG / RGNL (REGIONAL), CNTR, SYS / SYST and SRVCS / SRVS. PHYS is deliberately left alone (in the BMF it is mostly physical education). Because this changes name_key, it can change which EINs stage 1 matches, and np_normalize_signature() changes with it.
  • np_normalize() adds name_core, an exact-lookup key that drops connector words and legal forms anywhere in the name but keeps FOUNDATION, TRUST and FUND, so a charity and its foundation get different keys. np_name_core() computes it for raw strings.
  • np_normalize() adds name_placeholder, TRUE for names that are not names (“SEE SCHEDULE O”, “N/A”, no letters). np_block() gives such query rows no candidates. np_name_placeholder() checks raw strings.
  • np_name_rules() returns the normalization tables, for porting the rules to another engine such as a DuckDB SQL macro.

npmatch 0.1.0 (v0)

First tagged release (git tag v0.1.0). It pins the code that produced the combined 2025NOV + 2026MAY SAM-to-BMF crosswalk, so that crosswalk can be reproduced and cited against a fixed version of the package.

Results of the pinned run

Of 175,053 SAM nonprofit registrants, 141,420 (80.8%) are matched to an IRS BMF EIN:

matched by matches share of matches
stage 1 — probabilistic cascade 121,972 86.2%
stage 2 — LLM adjudication of MAYBEs 12,443 8.8%
stage 3 — LLM research of NOs 7,005 5.0%

The 33,633 unmatched registrants are mostly explained by stage 3: 12,892 are not nonprofits, 18,770 are nonprofits absent from this BMF vintage (mostly churches and foreign organizations), and 1,971 could not be determined.

What is in this release

Matching engine

  • A full record-linkage pipeline against the BMF: np_query() / np_reference() → np_normalize() → np_block() → np_compare() → np_score() → np_veto() → np_select() → np_tier() → np_route(), orchestrated by np_cascade() (multi-pass) or np_match() (single pass).
  • Nonprofit-specific normalization: abbreviation expansion, legal-suffix stripping, legal-form capture, and extraction of embedded numbers, ordinals and directions. np_normalize_signature() lets a cached artifact detect when normalization has drifted.
  • Progressive blocking passes: four exact name/DBA passes, then IDF-weighted name-token blocking within a state, a de-spaced-compound pass, and a cross-state pass. np_ref_index() tokenizes the reference once for reuse across passes and batches.
  • Hierarchical scoring (method = "hier"): name similarity plus the strongest confirmed geographic granularity, with a state-aware promotion for rare exact names.
  • A do-not-match veto engine (np_default_rules()): hard vetoes for number, ordinal and direction conflicts and for-profit legal forms; soft vetoes (cap at MAYBE) for affiliate-suffix mismatches and government entities.
  • YES / MAYBE / NO tiering with a near-tie margin and soft-veto demotion.

Running a project

  • Per-run project scaffolding: np_project_init(), np_project_use(), np_project_path() and np_project_status().
  • Stage drivers that share one outcome schema (np_stage_schema()): np_stage1_run() (batched cascade via np_run_batches()), np_stage2_run() (MAYBE adjudication hand-off), np_stage3_run() (NO research, with the np_entity_gate() screen) and np_final_run() (crosswalk, evaluation frame and funnel report).
  • np_merge_decisions() joins stage-2 adjudications back onto the review frame.

Review, labeling and training

  • Candidate-level review frames and LLM prompts: np_route(), np_as_prompt() / np_as_prompts(), np_review_report() (static HTML review report), np_label_frame(), np_calibration_frame() and np_veto_audit().
  • Model fitting and evaluation: np_train(), np_benchmark(), np_auc(), np_evaluate() and np_tune_thresholds().
  • Bundled data: npmatch_eval and npmatch_groundtruth, a hand-labeled 1,502-organization benchmark.

Data management

  • A data store with a manifest (np_data_init(), np_manifest()), source fetchers for the BMF and SAM extracts (np_fetch_bmf(), np_fetch_sam(), np_prepare_sam()), incremental diffs (np_diff_unmatched()) and run reports (np_run_report()).
  • Geography helpers: city aliases, HUD crosswalks, RUCA urbanicity and ZIP lookups.

Documentation

  • Articles: Workflow, Reviewer guide, Candidate evaluation frame, Training dataset and Building a classifier, published with the pkgdown site.
  • Reviewer workbook builds under dev/review-workbooks/: per-state themed evaluation workbooks, plus the stage-3 secondary review workbooks (all states, per state and zipped).

Known issues

  • Blocking misses. Of the 4,925 stage-3 matches that stage 1 never surfaced, 3,189 were never generated by blocking, 1,507 were scored but missed the shortlist, and 229 were hard-vetoed. final_ein_in_candset = 0 therefore mixes blocking, scoring and veto misses rather than marking blocking failures alone; the stage-3 secondary review separates them in stage1_pair_status.
  • Word-order sensitivity. Name similarity is Jaro-Winkler on the normalized name, so a reordered name (e.g. “BERNARDINO TELACU HOUSING SAN II” vs “TELACU HOUSING SAN BERNARDINO II”) can fall below the 0.85 floor. The order-insensitive overlap recovery only runs when the address already matches.
  • Fully vetoed registrants. For 5,226 registrants, stage 1 scored candidate pairs but the hard veto removed every one. They are flagged fully_vetoed in the secondary review for inspection. Among the 229 vetoed stage-3 matches, the for-profit legal-form rule accounts for 183.
  • Rollup anomaly. 126 stage3_research rows in the combined evaluation frame are NO_MATCH with an EIN but a blank final_ein; synthetic rows should only exist for matched registrants.
  • candidate_source = "none" rows come from the combined-run build, which is not part of the package; that value is not yet documented in the reviewer data dictionary.
